summary: After recalling the deaths of Aaron’s two sons, Leviticus 16 limits entry into the Most Holy Place and sets the annual atonement rite. Aaron bathes, wears linen, offers a bull for himself, uses one goat’s blood to cleanse the sanctuary, and sends a second goat into the wilderness bearing Israel’s confessed sins. The people observe the day with solemn rest and self-affliction while atonement is made for sanctuary, priests, and assembly.
whyItMatters: This chapter explains how a holy God can continue dwelling among a people whose uncleanness and transgressions reach even the sanctuary. Access is guarded, the priest also needs atonement, and the cleansing blood and departing goat address impurity and sin through distinct actions.

context.author: The text presents this instruction as Yahweh’s word through Moses; authorship and final composition are debated
context.audience: Aaron and succeeding high priests, together with the children of Israel and resident foreigners who observe the day
context.date: The rite is framed around Israel’s wilderness tabernacle; the date of final composition is debated
context.setting: The Tent of Meeting, especially the Most Holy Place within the veil, followed by the camp and wilderness
context.literaryForm: Priestly ritual instruction for the annual Day of Atonement

outline.heading: Restricted entry and priestly preparation
outline.note: Aaron may not enter whenever he chooses; animals, bathing, and linen garments prepare the annual approach.

outline.heading: Aaron’s bull and the two goats
outline.note: Aaron atones for his household, then lots distinguish the goat offered to Yahweh from the live scapegoat.

outline.heading: Blood and incense within the veil
outline.note: Incense shields the approach, and bull and goat blood cleanse the Holy Place, Tent, and altar from Israel’s uncleanness.

outline.heading: Confessed sins sent into the wilderness
outline.note: Aaron places both hands on the live goat, confesses Israel’s sins, and sends it to a solitary land.

outline.heading: Changing garments and completing the offerings
outline.note: Aaron bathes and changes before burnt offerings; those who release the goat or burn remains wash before returning.

outline.heading: The annual Sabbath of atonement
outline.note: Native and foreign resident cease work and afflict themselves while the anointed priest makes atonement once each year.

keyVerses.text: and Yahweh said to Moses, “Tell Aaron your brother not to come at just any time into the Most Holy Place within the veil, before the mercy seat which is on the ark; lest he die; for I will appear in the cloud on the mercy seat.
keyVerses.why: Entry within the veil is limited because the divine appearing makes approach dangerous.

keyVerses.text: He shall make atonement for the Holy Place, because of the uncleanness of the children of Israel, and because of their transgressions, even all their sins; and so he shall do for the Tent of Meeting that dwells with them in the middle of their uncleanness.
keyVerses.why: The Holy Place and Tent themselves receive atonement amid Israel’s uncleanness and sins.

keyVerses.text: Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, and confess over him all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions, even all their sins; and he shall put them on the head of the goat, and shall send him away into the wilderness by the hand of a man who is ready.
keyVerses.why: Confession and both hands place Israel’s offenses on the live goat before its removal.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin by recalling the deaths of Aaron’s sons?
questions.answer: Their deaths establish the danger behind the first command: Aaron may not enter the Most Holy Place whenever he chooses. The annual procedure is therefore not ornamental; it defines how the priest can approach the place of God’s appearing without dying.

questions.question: Why must Aaron first offer a bull for himself and his household?
questions.answer: The high priest does not stand outside Israel’s need for atonement. Before handling the people’s goat blood, he offers for himself and his house, and verse 17 again includes his own household before the whole assembly.

questions.question: What is the “mercy seat,” and why does incense cover it?
questions.answer: Within this chapter it is the place on the ark where Yahweh says he will appear in the cloud. Aaron brings a cloud of incense over it “so that he will not die,” then sprinkles blood there according to the commanded sequence.

questions.question: Why are two goats used for the people’s sin offering?
questions.answer: Lots assign different but connected functions. One goat is killed and its blood is brought within the veil to cleanse sacred space; the other remains alive, receives the confessed iniquities of Israel, and carries them away into the wilderness.

questions.question: What does “scapegoat” mean in the chapter itself?
questions.answer: The WEB calls the living animal the “scapegoat.” Interpreters differ over whether the Hebrew designation Azazel names a wilderness being, a place, or removal itself. Its identity is disputed, but the rite is explicit: the goat remains alive and carries confessed offenses to an isolated wilderness region.

questions.question: Why do the Holy Place, Tent, and altar need atonement?
questions.answer: Verse 16 says the Tent dwells among Israel’s uncleanness, transgressions, and sins, and verses 18-19 extend cleansing to the altar. The objects have not committed wrong; the rite cleanses sacred space from the defilement brought into its sphere.

questions.question: Does laying sins on the live goat make the animal morally guilty?
questions.answer: Aaron confesses Israel’s iniquities with both hands on the goat’s head, and the goat is assigned to carry them away. The animal remains alive when it is released in the wilderness; the rite describes removal of the community’s offenses rather than an offense committed by the animal.

questions.question: Why are bathing, clothing changes, and washing required at several points?
questions.answer: The chapter does not give a separate symbolism for each washing or clothing change. In its sequence, Aaron bathes before the linen garments and again before his regular garments; the men who release the goat or burn the remains also wash before reentering the camp.

questions.question: What are the people commanded to do on this annual day?
questions.answer: On the tenth day of the seventh month, native-born and resident foreigner stop work and “afflict” themselves while atonement is made. The day is a Sabbath of solemn rest. These verses command self-affliction without specifying its actions in detail.

glossary.def: The inner sanctuary within the veil, containing the ark and mercy seat and entered under strict limits.
The WEB’s term for the live goat assigned to the disputed designation la-Azazel and sent away bearing Israel’s confessed sins.
The rites that cleanse priest, people, and sacred space and address Israel’s sins before Yahweh.

reviewer: Codex editorial agents; independent chapter review

before.text: Rules for male and female bodily discharges close with a warning against defiling the tabernacle. The annual rite now addresses the holy spaces that stand among Israel’s uncleanness and sins.

here.text: Aaron’s preparation, blood rites, and the release of the live goat distinguish cleansing the sanctuary from carrying confessed offenses away. The community marks the annual day with rest and self-affliction.

after.text: The next chapter regulates slaughter and sacrifice at the Tent, rejects goat-idol offerings, and explains the prohibition on consuming life-bearing blood.
